text.p: Malaysia's power utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd on Thursday reported a group net profit of 797.8 million ringgit ($316 million) for the year ended August 31, 1996, down 36 percent from 1.24 billion ringgit in the previous year.
This was well below market forecasts of between 1.0 billion to 1.2 billion ringgit, analysts said.
The Estimate Directory of analysts' consensus forecasts had put Tenaga's net earnings at an average of 1.13 billion ringgit.
Net earnings per share fell to 25.9 cents from 40.7 cents, while turnover increased to 8.15 billion ringgit from 6.86 billion.

Tenaga said in its financial statement the substantial reduction in profits was principally due to increased purchases of electricity from private power companies, known as Independent Power Producers (IPPs) -- up by 1.22 billion ringgit or 114 percent over the previous year.
Tenaga paid a total 2.275 billion ringgit for electricity to the IPPs in the 1995/96 financial year, compared with some analysts' forecast of 2.0 billion ringgit.
Another reason for the drop in profits was the "provision for payment of rebates, interest on customer deposit and unexpected non-recurrence expenses," Tenaga's statement said.
Tenaga has agreed to provide 70 million ringgit in rebates to its customers as compensation for an August 3 blackout over much of Malaysia that lasted up to 15 hours.
The component designated "other operating expenses", which accounted for 7.77 percent of total expenses this year, amounted to 599 million ringgit.
Tenaga did not say what the expenses were. But it was a 70 percent increase over the previous financial year, said a power analyst at a local bank-backed securities house.
"We were expecting the profit to be lower but we did not expect it to be this bad," said Adin Jarjis, power analyst at Pesaka Jardine Fleming.
He said Tenaga's stock would weaken further on Friday. "We had the stock on sell even before the results," he said.
Tenaga's shares fell 50 cents to 10.50 ringgit on Thursday. The stock accounts for nearly 15 percent of the weightage on the key Composite Index of the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange.
Some analysts said the stock may still find favour after the government expressed support for the state-run power company.
The government, which has a 70 percent stake in Tenaga, has made a series of announcements in the last two weeks which showed they are supporting the utility, analysts said.
"We know the government is helping Tenaga. At this point, I'm neutral on the stock," said Phua Lee Kerk, an analyst at Vickers Ballas Research.
"If the stock drops to 10 ringgit, we may see some buying on weakness," he said.
Last week, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said Tenaga, and not the private power companies, would get the bigger role in new electricity generation projects.

Responding to Tenaga complaints that its profits were being eroded by the prices it pays to buy electricity from IPPs, the government also said that IPPs would have to help bear the costs of supplying power to rural areas. ($1 = 2.52 ringgit)
